title: Ultimatum

jokes.text: Dwight presiding over a 'Knights of the Night' meeting in the office, reading official minutes aloud as 'Secretary Schrute'
jokes.setup: A seemingly formal meeting opens with official-sounding language — 'Secretary Schrute will read the minutes from previous meeting'
jokes.punchline: The group is called 'Knights of the Night,' a volunteer crime patrol that Dwight is running with bureaucratic seriousness
jokes.explanation: This scores high on character integration because only Dwight would form a volunteer crime patrol, give it a medieval name, and appoint himself secretary. The bureaucratic framing (reading official minutes) layered over the absurd content is classic Office comedy. Earns its score because it's pure Dwight logic, not a random joke.

jokes.text: Dwight explains the Knights of the Night: 'We're often compared to the Guardian Angels, but we could not be more different from them. Seriously, we are nothing like the Guardian Angels. I mean, broad strokes purposes, sure. Think Guardian Angels.'
jokes.setup: Dwight emphatically insists Knights of the Night are nothing like the Guardian Angels
jokes.punchline: He immediately concedes they're basically the same thing: 'broad strokes purposes, sure. Think Guardian Angels.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structure: the triple insistence followed by immediate self-contradiction is a perfect comedic reversal. The economy is tight — each sentence builds then collapses. Pure Dwight: his pride demands differentiation but his honesty compels him to admit sameness. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: 'One of our many recent good deeds, we set out to capture the Scranton Strangler. Mission accomplished. Not by us.'
jokes.setup: Dwight proudly announces a major crime-fighting success
jokes.punchline: Immediately deflates it: 'Not by us.' — they had nothing to do with it
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — three words ('Not by us') destroy the previous boast with surgical precision. The structure is perfect: build-up, false triumph, immediate deflation. Highly quotable, usable in everyday contexts. References the Scranton Strangler running gag, adds resonance. One of the best jokes in the episode and among the better Office cold opens.

jokes.text: Jim wanders into the Knights of the Night meeting claiming to look for his BlackBerry; Dwight immediately assumes Jim is there to mock him
jokes.setup: Jim nonchalantly says he's just looking for his phone and to 'carry on'
jokes.punchline: Dwight, hyper-aware of Jim's pranking history, launches into a preemptive defense: 'No, no, no, no. I see how this movie ends. You make fun of me, everyone laughs. Ha, ha, ha. Screw you.'
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy rooted in years of established Jim-Dwight dynamic. Dwight's paranoia is entirely earned by their history. 'I see how this movie ends' is a nice line. Slightly undercut because it's familiar territory.

jokes.text: "No, no, no, no, no. I see how this movie ends. You make fun of me, everyone laughs. Ha, ha, ha. Screw you."
jokes.setup: Jim has stumbled into the meeting; Dwight anticipates mockery
jokes.punchline: Dwight preemptively narrates the entire comedic arc of what's about to happen and tells Jim off before it even starts
jokes.explanation: A smart meta moment — Dwight is self-aware enough to know the comedic dynamic he's always trapped in, which is itself funny. It almost breaks the fourth wall without quite doing so. 'Screw you' as the button is unexpectedly blunt and earns a laugh. Good character integration.

jokes.text: A fellow Knight mocks Jim doing an impression of their leader's 'weird voice': 'You gonna make fun of our leader's weird voice, huh? Dwight, don't be bothered...' — and Dwight snaps 'Over the line, Jim.'
jokes.setup: A Knight defensively impersonates Jim impersonating their leader's voice to prove a point about mockery
jokes.punchline: In doing so, he mocks the voice himself, and Dwight blames Jim anyway
jokes.explanation: Nice layered irony — the defender does the very thing he's defending against. Dwight's 'Over the line, Jim' misdirects blame hilariously. Good structural joke but not particularly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight reads from the minutes: 'Knights stayed outside to play flashlight tag.' Jim: 'Oh, come on. That sounds awesome.' Dwight: 'It was pretty cool.' Jim: 'Was it?' Dwight: 'It was fun... It was pretty awesome.'
jokes.setup: Dwight reads minutes of supposedly serious crime-patrol activity; Jim pokes fun at flashlight tag
jokes.punchline: Dwight genuinely, warmly admits it was pretty awesome — the guard drops completely and he and Jim have a brief moment of sincere agreement
jokes.explanation: The warmth of the payoff elevates this beyond a simple gag. The comedy of Dwight dropping all defensiveness and genuinely bonding with Jim over how fun flashlight tag was is sweet and character-driven. The incremental admission ('pretty cool... it was fun... it was pretty awesome') mirrors how someone actually caves to genuine enthusiasm. Rewatch bonus for the brief Jim-Dwight moment.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'January 3, 2011. A day which will live infamously.'
jokes.setup: Michael opens with dramatic gravitas, clearly echoing FDR's 'Day of Infamy' speech
jokes.punchline: 'Infamously' — malapropism mixing 'infamous' and 'infamy,' delivered with complete unironic solemnity
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott — the grandiose historical reference mangled by a near-miss word. 'Infamously' instead of 'infamy' is a Michael Scott signature move. Well-integrated into character. Not the funniest example of his malapropisms but sets the emotional stakes of the episode.

jokes.text: Michael describes Holly as 'otherwise known as a living, breathing angel'
jokes.setup: Michael is building up Holly's name with increasingly hyperbolic nicknames
jokes.punchline: 'a living, breathing angel' — the escalating absurdity of his devotion delivered deadpan as an official designation
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy showing Michael's absurd level of adoration. Works in context but not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Michael has made a video of himself talking himself down — 'nobody talks me down like myself in a video talking me down'
jokes.setup: Michael acknowledges he'll need to be talked down from an extreme emotional reaction
jokes.punchline: His solution is a pre-recorded video of himself giving himself advice — and he's completely confident this is the best possible option
jokes.explanation: Deeply Michael Scott — the logic that no one is better at managing Michael than Michael himself, so the solution is a video of Michael advising Michael. It's absurd but internally consistent with his narcissism and genuine emotional need. High character integration; only Michael would do this and believe in it completely.

jokes.text: On the self-help video, Michael-on-tape says: 'Holly is engaged to somebody else and you want to kill yourself. That may seem like a good idea, but it's not.'
jokes.setup: Michael has pre-recorded advice for his worst-case scenario emotional state
jokes.punchline: 'That may seem like a good idea, but it's not' — delivered as earnest counsel against suicide, treating it as a reasonable impulse that just needs a talking-out
jokes.explanation: Dark but calibrated perfectly for Michael's character — he's not actually suicidal, he's being melodramatic, and the joke is that he counsels himself against it with the gentlest, most matter-of-fact framing. 'That may seem like a good idea, but it's not' is a great line. Economy is excellent. Genuinely funny dark comedy.

jokes.text: Michael-on-tape says '...it's not' and present-Michael mishears it as 'snot,' starts laughing. 'Sorry, it sounded like you said it's snot.'
jokes.setup: Michael is watching his own serious emotional self-help video at a critical moment
jokes.punchline: He breaks the solemnity by giggling at a mishearing — 'snot' — completely undercutting the gravity
jokes.explanation: Silly but effective. Michael cracking himself up during his own serious self-help video is perfectly in character — his emotional range is genuinely childlike. The 'snot' beat punctures the melodrama nicely. Not a sophisticated joke but executed with good timing.

jokes.text: Pam introduces the Resolution Board — 'Wow, did your baby draw that? The glitter is blinding.'
jokes.setup: Pam enthusiastically presents her handmade Resolution Board as an office morale initiative
jokes.punchline: A coworker immediately roasts the childlike quality of the glittery board by asking if her baby made it
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional gag. 'Did your baby draw that?' is a decent burn. Not exceptional but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: she mentions the cool office administrator Sue at Vance Refrigeration, then cut to: 'I know Sue, she's not that great. And you know her husband's in a wheelchair, right?'
jokes.setup: Pam admiringly describes Sue's awesome morale wall and says 'Sue just goes for it. She's awesome.'
jokes.punchline: An offscreen voice immediately undercuts with 'she's not that great' — and then offers the non-sequitur character attack that her husband is in a wheelchair as if that's relevant criticism
jokes.explanation: The wheelchair non-sequitur is a nice dark beat — it's presented as a strike against Sue's coolness when it's obviously irrelevant and slightly cruel, which is the joke. Good economy and structure. The offense is mild enough to land as dark humor rather than genuine cruelty.

jokes.text: Erin goes through happy/sad items: 'Sponge — sad. To soak up my tears.' / 'Gummy bears and gummy worms — bears sad, worms happy. Come on, Erin.'
jokes.setup: Michael has prepared happy items and sad items for any emotional outcome regarding Holly
jokes.punchline: Erin can't tell which items belong in which category; Michael has very specific emotional logic (bears = sad, worms = happy) that only makes sense to him
jokes.explanation: Charming and specific. The internal logic of 'bears sad, worms happy' is wonderfully absurd, and Michael's exasperated 'Come on, Erin' implies this is self-evident to him. Good character work for both Michael and Erin.

jokes.text: Ukuleles: Erin guesses 'Happy?' — Michael: 'Sad. Something to break.'
jokes.setup: Erin continues categorizing emotional supplies, guessing ukuleles are happy
jokes.punchline: 'Sad. Something to break.' — Michael plans to smash a ukulele in grief
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — four words deliver a complete, absurd emotional image. Ukuleles are inherently cheerful instruments, making them the perfect object of premeditated grief destruction. Fully earned by Michael's character; he would absolutely plan this. One of the sharpest small jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Two bottles of scotch. Both sad.' Erin: 'And did you get the tickets?' Michael: 'Two front row center to Paula Poundstone, live in Poughkeepsie. Holly's favorite.'
jokes.setup: Michael has prepared gifts and alcohol for either emotional outcome
jokes.punchline: Paula Poundstone is the comedian he's chosen to celebrate — a very specific, left-field choice that signals Michael's slightly dated pop culture taste
jokes.explanation: Paula Poundstone is a good specific choice — dated enough to be funny, real enough to be grounded. The 'both sad' scotch line is also clean. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael imagines being called up on stage by Paula Poundstone: 'I hope she doesn't call us up on stage, that would suck. Hey, you think you could do my job better? I don't know. What's your name? Michael.'
jokes.setup: Michael is excited about Paula Poundstone tickets but adds a caveat
jokes.punchline: His fear of audience participation is expressed through an imagined exchange that reveals his low self-esteem masked as humility — he actually does fear being shown up
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment but a bit rambling. The imagined audience-participation sequence reveals character anxiety but the joke itself isn't especially tight.

jokes.text: Talking head about Holly: 'if not, he'll be avoiding the biggest mistake of his life'
jokes.setup: A coworker says they're excited for Michael either way — if Holly chooses him he'll be happy
jokes.punchline: The other outcome is framed not as heartbreak but as Michael 'avoiding the biggest mistake of his life' — implying they don't think Holly is right for him or that Michael is bad at relationships
jokes.explanation: Subtle irony — framing Holly as a potential mistake cuts against the show's romantic framing of the relationship. Works as dark background commentary. Not particularly sharp but functions.

jokes.text: Holly arrives — Michael tries to see if she has a ring by manufacturing an elaborate mitten handshake sequence: 'Those are so fuzzy and warm. Let me feel those... Put her there. Give me a good firm one... You're hired.'
jokes.setup: Michael desperately needs to know if Holly is wearing an engagement ring, but can't ask directly — she's wearing mittens
jokes.punchline: He escalates to a fake professional 'You're hired' handshake to try to get her to remove the mittens, which is completely transparent and absurd
jokes.explanation: Physically inventive and rooted in character. Michael's inability to be subtle or direct collides with genuine romantic desperation. The 'You're hired' line is wonderfully absurd. Good cringe potential.

jokes.text: Jim to Michael, re: the thermostat scheme: 'Hey, hey, hey. Want me to crank the thermostat to 90? Smoke her out? She can't keep those mittens on forever.' Michael: 'Yes. No, what? Stop. Yes.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to see Holly's ring finger through mittens; Jim joins the absurdity
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'Yes. No, what? Stop. Yes.' — his simultaneous moral hesitation and desperate agreement
jokes.explanation: 'Yes. No, what? Stop. Yes.' is a beautifully economical line capturing Michael's rapid internal conflict. Also sweet that Jim is actively helping rather than mocking. The rhythm of the line is great.

jokes.text: Michael sees no ring on Holly's hand and realizes she's NOT engaged — 'Oh, I get it. Everybody knows about the ultimatum.' Holly: 'Yes, I told everyone.' Michael: 'Ha! Hey, right back at you, bitch.'
jokes.setup: Michael realizes the office knows about the AJ ultimatum situation; Holly confirms she told everyone
jokes.punchline: 'Ha! Hey, right back at you, bitch.' — Michael's bizarre, aggressive celebration directed at Holly for no clear reason
jokes.explanation: 'Right back at you, bitch' directed lovingly at the woman he adores, as a celebration, is quintessential Michael Scott absurdity. It makes no logical sense but perfect character sense — he's so overwhelmed with joy that his social filters collapse completely. Highly quotable, high character integration.

jokes.text: Michael's pure joy explosion — 'Happy, happy, happy, happy!' followed by a physical freakout requiring multiple people to restrain him
jokes.setup: Michael discovers Holly is not engaged and loses all composure
jokes.punchline: He erupts into a full physical celebration that requires intervention — 'Whoa, whoa, whoa! Calm down! Breathe.'
jokes.explanation: Broad physical comedy that works in the moment but is less interesting analytically. Steve Carell's physical performance sells it. The setup of elaborate emotional preparation pays off in the chaos.

jokes.text: 'Wait a second. Are you listening to music?' — Michael has headphones in during his emotional breakdown and is ignoring advice
jokes.setup: People are trying to calm Michael down; he seems unresponsive to instructions
jokes.punchline: He's been listening to music the whole time, not hearing the advice at all
jokes.explanation: Good visual reveal joke. Michael managing his own emotions with a personal soundtrack while others try to help him is very character-consistent. Clean structure.

jokes.text: Office dance-off erupts in the bullpen — 'Michael dance-off!' with various employees joining in
jokes.setup: Michael's emotional release transitions from crisis to celebration; coworkers join his dancing
jokes.punchline: The entire office spontaneously breaks into a dance-off, which is presented as a normal resolution to emotional crisis
jokes.explanation: Fun sequence, earns emotional goodwill, but not a sharp joke structurally. Works better as a mood moment than comedy. Functional.

jokes.text: Dwight refuses to write a resolution: 'Not doing that.' Pam: 'Why not?' Dwight: 'I've achieved plenty, and there's no better than the best.'
jokes.setup: Pam is collecting resolution cards from everyone
jokes.punchline: Dwight declines because he's already perfected himself — 'there's no better than the best' — delivered without irony
jokes.explanation: Concise and perfectly Dwight. His unironic self-assessment as having achieved perfection is a great character beat. 'There's no better than the best' is quotable and perfectly delivered deadpan.

jokes.text: Kevin's resolution card: 'Learn to cook for one.' Talking head: 'I love cooking. But I always find myself throwing out half the food... So I figured it's time to just start preparing the right amount of food for the right number of people, which is one.' 'Well, maybe you'll meet someone.' 'No, some people just don't meet someone. I'm fine with it. Really. This is not a pity party. It's not a party at all. It's just sad.'
jokes.setup: Kevin shares his resolution which seems practical at first
jokes.punchline: The escalating clarifications — 'This is not a pity party. It's not a party at all. It's just sad.' — reveal deep loneliness while Kevin insists he's totally fine
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating self-reassurance ('I'm fine with it. Really. This is not a pity party. It's not a party at all. It's just sad.') is structurally superb — each correction makes it worse. 'It's not a party at all. It's just sad.' is a perfect, quotable line. The joke earns genuine pathos while remaining funny. High originality for a simple premise executed with precision.

jokes.text: Angela's resolution: 'Make time for romance.' Jim: 'Who's the senator?' Angela: 'My boyfriend.' Jim: 'Oh, you mean the state senator. I'm sorry, I was confused 'cause you accidentally wrote The senator.'
jokes.setup: Angela's resolution is to make time for romance; she mentions 'The senator' as her boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Jim sarcastically apologizes for being 'confused' by her inflated title for her boyfriend — she wrote 'The senator' with capital-T gravity
jokes.explanation: Nice subtle dig at Angela's pretension. The joke hinges on the capital-T 'The senator' — she treats him as THE senator, as if there's only one. Jim's mock confusion is clean and economical. Good character work.

jokes.text: "No, some people just don't meet someone. I'm fine with it. Really. This is not a pity party."
jokes.setup: Pam tries to be optimistic about Kevin meeting someone
jokes.punchline: Kevin's three-sentence denial of sadness is itself a perfect portrait of quiet sadness — especially 'This is not a pity party. It's not a party at all. It's just sad.'
jokes.explanation: The best Kevin moment in the episode and one of the episode's top jokes. 'This is not a pity party. It's not a party at all. It's just sad.' is beautifully structured — each sentence contracts the space a little further until you're left with pure sadness. The correction of 'pity party' to just 'sad' is linguistically precise and emotionally devastating. Comparable in craft to the show's best 'cringe-poignant' jokes.

jokes.text: Darryl's resolution exchange: 'Wait, wait, wait. It's that easy? That's not a resolution. That's just something I wanna do. Okay, fine. I can do that.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests an easy resolution and Darryl initially objects that it's too simple
jokes.punchline: He immediately accepts it anyway — 'Okay, fine. I can do that.' — proving his own point
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional joke about how easily we lower our standards for resolutions. Good economy, relatable, but doesn't stretch beyond the obvious observation.

jokes.text: Michael's resolution: 'Meet a loose woman.' Andy immediately: 'Oh, God. That's a good one. Yeah? You know what? That's my new one. I'm taking that one, too.'
jokes.setup: Michael announces his New Year's resolution in the resolution card session
jokes.punchline: 'Meet a loose woman' — absurdly blunt and inappropriate for an HR context, which Andy enthusiastically co-opts
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'loose woman' is a great dated/absurd word choice from Michael. Andy's immediate enthusiastic adoption is a good escalation beat. The double-cringe of both Michael and Andy sharing this goal is earned.

jokes.text: Darryl's imagined bookstore pickup script: 'Hey, what book is that? Cool, let's hang out tonight. Sex already? Whoa.'
jokes.setup: Darryl suggests the bookstore as a great place to meet women and promises to show them how
jokes.punchline: His idealized pickup script accelerates at an impossible pace — from 'what book is that' to 'sex already? Whoa' in three exchanges
jokes.explanation: 'Sex already? Whoa.' is a perfectly economical, perfectly timed absurdist punchline. The compressed timeline of the fantasy — from introduction to sex in three beats — is funny on its own, and 'Sex already? Whoa' is quotable and delivers a great comic rhythm. Strong economy score.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head: 'My resolution is to read more. And if someone else is driving me to the book store, I can eat my PB and J in the car. 2011 is coming up all Darryl.'
jokes.setup: Darryl declares his bookstore plan is actually a resolution strategy
jokes.punchline: '2011 is coming up all Darryl' — delivered with complete sincerity about what is a very modest set of plans
jokes.explanation: '2011 is coming up all Darryl' is a great line — the self-satisfied declaration of victory over very minor logistics. High quotability, great character integration (Darryl's laid-back confidence), and perfectly economical. One of the episode's most memorable lines.

jokes.text: Holly has a new phone; Michael does an elaborate E.T. bit to communicate with her. 'E.T. phone Holly. Holly like phone? Holly misses old phone.' Holly plays along. Kelly: 'Oh, God. Please stop.'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Holly with a new phone and uses the opportunity to interact
jokes.punchline: He does a full E.T. impression as a flirtation device; Kelly's 'Oh, God. Please stop.' voices the audience reaction
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael cringe flirting. The E.T. bit is slightly dated humor but character-consistent — Michael communicating through pop culture references as emotional shorthand. Kelly's reaction is the payoff. Good cringe but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jim's phone call with Pam — clearly a domestic conversation about movies — ending with 'I love you, too.' The camera lingers on the phone.
jokes.setup: Jim is on the phone having a mundane conversation about which movie to see
jokes.punchline: The contrast between the total normalcy of this domestic phone call and the romantic chaos in the office around him; the camera beat emphasizes the counterpoint
jokes.explanation: Subtle contextual joke — Jim and Pam's settled domesticity contrasted against the romantic chaos around Holly/Michael. More of a tonal beat than a joke, but functions as quiet comedy.

jokes.text: Michael to Jim about Holly: 'Do you think she's already dating a different A.J.?' Jim: 'I don't think so.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to understand Holly's confusing behavior
jokes.punchline: Michael's leap that she might have immediately switched to another man named A.J. is a perfect absurdist non-solution born of desperate magical thinking
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of 'a different A.J.' — not just another man, but specifically another A.J. — is the joke. It shows Michael's mind reaching for the least threatening explanation. Jim's flat 'I don't think so' is perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: Michael: 'she would think of me as her friend. Oh, hi, friend.' — said with complete horror
jokes.setup: Michael worries about approaching Holly about AJ
jokes.punchline: Being Holly's friend is framed as a fate worse than death — 'Oh, hi, friend' delivered with existential dread
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. Michael's horror at friendship is purely from his perspective — not insulting to Holly, just his all-or-nothing romantic worldview. 'Oh, hi, friend.' with the horror behind it is a nice delivery.

jokes.text: Jim suggests Pam talk to Holly; Michael: 'You think she'd talk to you?' Jim: 'Why wouldn't she?' Michael: 'That's true, she's really nice. She'd talk to anybody.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks skeptically whether Holly would talk to Pam
jokes.punchline: His explanation pivots from implied insult to accidental compliment — Holly would talk to Pam not because Pam is special but because Holly is indiscriminately nice
jokes.explanation: Nice double-pivot — Michael seems to be insulting Pam but is actually complimenting Holly with a backhanded qualifier. The logic is perfect Michael Scott: well-intentioned, thoughtless, and completely unaware. Clean execution.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'All right, we should divide up by section. I will take Romance and Travel.' Andy: 'I'll take the entirety of the second floor.' Michael: 'I got that cutie behind the counter.'
jokes.setup: The men are strategizing at the bookstore for meeting women
jokes.punchline: Each character's 'territory' reveals their personality: Darryl is practical, Andy overreaches hilariously ('the entirety of the second floor'), and Michael has already zeroed in on one specific person
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble character comedy. 'The entirety of the second floor' from Andy is the standout beat — the scale is absurd. All three choices reveal character efficiently.

jokes.text: Andy and Darryl pretend to be bookstore employees: 'Well, if you read a lot you should check out our e-readers. They're really neat.' Darryl: 'Oh, I work at a paper company. Those things terrify me. They could put us out of business.' Worker: 'Heard those machines hold, like, 10 books at once.' 'Actually, it's 10,000.' 'Holy [bleep]. What?'
jokes.setup: Andy and Darryl are pretending to work at the bookstore to impress a woman
jokes.punchline: Darryl breaks character to have a genuine paper-industry anxiety attack about e-readers, then discovers they hold 10,000 books — 'Holy [bleep]. What?' — his crisis deepens
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered: the absurdity of pretending to be employees, Darryl's paper-industry existential dread breaking through, and the escalation of '10 books? No, 10,000.' 'Holy [bleep]. What?' is a great reaction. Character integration is excellent — Darryl's Dunder Mifflin identity collision with the digital age is earned comedy.

jokes.text: 'So light. Like a croissant.' — Darryl holding the e-reader with wonder
jokes.setup: Darryl has just been horrified by e-readers and now holds one
jokes.punchline: 'So light. Like a croissant.' — the awe shifts his existential dread to childlike wonder, conveyed through a completely left-field food comparison
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — 'So light. Like a croissant.' is four words that create a perfect, specific, unexpected image. The croissant comparison is surprising and oddly precise. It's the kind of line that makes a writers' room erupt. High quotability, high originality for such a simple delivery. One of the episode's best pure joke lines.

jokes.text: After pretending to be employees: 'Why did we pretend like we work here?' 'Is that what we were doing?' 'I don't know...'
jokes.setup: The bookstore employee leaves and the men drop the pretense
jokes.punchline: Neither can explain why they did it; 'Is that what we were doing?' implies they didn't even consciously decide to
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware beat after the absurdity. The lack of explanation is the joke. 'Is that what we were doing?' has a nice bewildered quality.

jokes.text: 'How'd you do?' 'Good. Yeah. Good, real good. Yeah. I think we kind of nailed it. Yeah, pretty much. But you know, this place is kind of tapped out.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks how the men did meeting women at the bookstore
jokes.punchline: Their bullish self-assessment ('we kind of nailed it') followed by immediate retreat ('this place is kind of tapped out') signals total failure while saving face
jokes.explanation: The face-saving pivot is a recognizable social maneuver executed with good comic rhythm. 'This place is kind of tapped out' is a great line for someone who absolutely did not nail it.

jokes.text: Michael's book haul: 'What'd you get? A book about oceans. Oh, really? What else? Let me see. That's porn. Pornography. Old lady. Nasty porn.'
jokes.setup: The men compare what books they got at the bookstore
jokes.punchline: Michael has purchased old-lady-targeted pornography, escalating through three increasingly descriptive labels: 'That's porn. Pornography. Old lady. Nasty porn.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'That's porn' to 'Old lady. Nasty porn.' is well-paced. Each designation adds a worse quality. Specifically 'old lady' porn is an unexpected detail. Clean escalation structure.

jokes.text: Michael approaches a woman reading alone: 'Follow my lead. Hey, want some company? Want some company?' — two identical approaches to two different women
jokes.setup: Michael declares 'follow my lead' and approaches a woman at the bookstore
jokes.punchline: His technique is simply repeating the same opener verbatim at a second woman, with the same result — inviting himself to sit down with no additional charm
jokes.explanation: The double-opener is mildly amusing — his 'technique' is just repetition of the most minimal possible approach. Functional cringe.

jokes.text: Pam asks Holly: 'Not even for a week to make him buy you a present?'
jokes.setup: Pam is pressing Holly about why she didn't break up with AJ even briefly after the ultimatum expired
jokes.punchline: Pam's casual suggestion that a week-long fake breakup to extract a gift is a perfectly reasonable option — delivered as if this is an obvious strategy
jokes.explanation: Pam's cynical-but-cheerful suggestion subverts her usually idealistic romantic persona in a funny way. The line is economical and gets a good laugh from the matter-of-fact delivery.

jokes.text: Dwight at the strip club entrance: 'I've never been in one before. I'm tired of being Mr. Perfect Role Model all the time.'
jokes.setup: The men are supposed to be going back to the office; Dwight refuses
jokes.punchline: 'I'm tired of being Mr. Perfect Role Model all the time.' — Dwight self-designating as a role model that everyone looks to for moral guidance, which nobody does
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight self-perception joke. 'Mr. Perfect Role Model' is the exact phrase only Dwight would use unironically. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Darryl on the day-shift strip club: 'I got nothing against strip clubs, but I do have something against them at noon on a Monday. The day shift at a strip club? You can't un-see that.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants to go to a strip club instead of returning to the office
jokes.punchline: 'The day shift at a strip club? You can't un-see that.' — Darryl's pragmatic warning about the specific horrors of afternoon strip clubs
jokes.explanation: 'You can't un-see that' is a perfect, highly quotable line. The specificity of 'noon on a Monday' elevating it from a general strip-club joke to a precise commentary is excellent. Darryl's dry authority sells it completely. One of Darryl's best lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Darryl's rapid-fire list of who goes roller skating: 'Single moms at a skating party. Sweet 16, 10-year reunion parties. Chicks fall down, need help getting back up. Roller derby practice.'
jokes.setup: Darryl pitches a roller rink as an alternative venue for meeting women
jokes.punchline: His increasingly specific and random categorization of rink demographics culminates in 'roller derby practice' — women who would destroy them
jokes.explanation: Good list comedy with escalating incongruity. 'Chicks fall down, need help getting back up' as a seduction strategy is specific and absurd. The roller derby kicker undercuts the whole premise.

jokes.text: Erin's resolution update: 'My goal was to learn a new word every single day. And I must say that it is going immensely.'
jokes.setup: Erin shares progress on her resolution to learn a new word every day
jokes.punchline: 'It is going immensely' — she means 'tremendously' or 'immensely well,' but uses 'immensely' as an adjective/adverb incorrectly, proving she hasn't actually learned to use words properly
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: Erin's resolution is to learn words, and in reporting her success she demonstrates she hasn't learned to use words correctly. 'It is going immensely' as a standalone statement with misused vocabulary is a layered, self-undermining joke. High marks across the board — it's elegant, character-specific (only Erin), and rewards close listening. The irony is completely earned.

jokes.text: Gabe intercepts the gift from Sabre meant for Erin — 'Intercepted. Hey... Gabe.' 'Oops-e-doops.'
jokes.setup: A Sabre company gift is handed to Erin for her resolution progress
jokes.punchline: Gabe snatches it mid-handoff with proprietary glee, then says 'Oops-e-doops' when caught — an attempt at adorable self-deprecation that is aggressively unfunny
jokes.explanation: 'Oops-e-doops' is a perfectly chosen phrase for Gabe — it's the most uncharismatic possible response, revealing his social awkwardness while trying to be charming. Good character work.

jokes.text: Creed's resolution: 'I want to do a cartwheel. But real casual, like. Not make a big deal out of it. But I know everybody saw it, just one stunning, gorgeous cartwheel.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Creed what his resolution is
jokes.punchline: Creed wants to do a casual, unnoticed cartwheel — but simultaneously wants everyone to see it and find it 'stunning and gorgeous'; the mutually exclusive desires are stated without self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Creed joke. The simultaneous desire for casualness ('not make a big deal out of it') and desperate need for an audience ('I know everybody saw it, just one stunning, gorgeous cartwheel') is perfectly contradictory and completely in character. Creed's mysterious, self-contained world makes this feel inevitable. High character integration, high originality. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: Kevin's resolution confession: 'Since last year I ate none.' (re: vegetables)
jokes.setup: Pam confesses she hasn't eaten more vegetables yet but still has time; others confess similar small failures
jokes.punchline: Kevin's confession obliterates the others — he hasn't eaten a single vegetable in an entire year
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words ('Since last year... none') that completely puncture the confessional format. The escalation from 'I haven't started yet' to 'I've eaten zero vegetables in twelve months' is perfectly timed. Character-specific to Kevin's magnificent dietary disasters.

jokes.text: Dwight confesses he had a sip of coffee but insists it's fine: 'with all of your support, by this time next year maybe I'll be down to one glass of iced tea a week.' Then: 'Next year? Come on. I mean, what is the point? What is the point of that?'
jokes.setup: Dwight confesses a minor coffee infraction but frames it as progress
jokes.punchline: His optimistic 10-year timeline for caffeine reduction is met with Michael's genuine exasperated 'What is the point?' — correctly identifying that Dwight's goal is absurdly inefficient
jokes.explanation: Good Dwight-Michael inversion — usually Dwight is the competent one being mocked, here Michael correctly calls out Dwight's ridiculous timeline. 'What is the point of that?' lands well.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I made a resolution to floss. And I did it. 12:01, January 1st. Bam! Blood everywhere.'
jokes.setup: Michael holds himself up as an example of resolution success
jokes.punchline: 'Bam! Blood everywhere.' — he flossed so aggressively on January 1st that he bled significantly, treating this as a triumph
jokes.explanation: 'Bam! Blood everywhere.' is a great punchy line. The timestamp '12:01' adds specificity that implies premeditation and earnestness. Michael treating a violent flossing incident as a success story is perfect character comedy. High economy.

jokes.text: Michael snaps at everyone failing their resolutions: 'What is wrong with you people? Can't you stick to anything? Not all of us are Michael Freaking Scott.' — then orders Erin to get vegetables and Creed to do a cartwheel immediately
jokes.setup: Michael has been listening to everyone confess their failures and reaches his limit
jokes.punchline: 'Not all of us are Michael Freaking Scott' — Michael refers to himself in the third person as a benchmark of human excellence in response to a mediocre flossing achievement
jokes.explanation: 'Not all of us are Michael Freaking Scott' is a very quotable line because it's simultaneously self-aggrandizing and absurdly modest — the achievement being referenced is simply flossing once. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Well, I can't. I don't know how.' Michael: 'You're just going to somersault around for the rest of your life. And you know what's gonna be on your tombstone? Loser.' Creed: 'My tombstone's already made, thank you.'
jokes.setup: Michael demands Creed do a cartwheel; Creed admits he doesn't know how
jokes.punchline: 'My tombstone's already made, thank you.' — Creed has a pre-made tombstone, delivered as a mild corrective point in a heated argument, as if this is perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Creed joke. 'My tombstone's already made, thank you' is dropped into an argument about cartwheels with complete casual matter-of-factness — no explanation, no elaboration. The joke implies tremendous backstory (who pre-makes their tombstone? why does Creed have one?) while delivering zero answers. Perfect economy, perfect character integration. One of the top three jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Kevin being force-fed broccoli: 'Why are you eating stem first?' Kevin: 'This is a new food for me. How else should I eat it?' Gabe: 'The other way.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is being made to eat broccoli as Michael enforces the resolution
jokes.punchline: 'This is a new food for me.' — broccoli, a universally known vegetable, is described as a new food, confirming he truly has never eaten vegetables
jokes.explanation: Great callback payoff to Kevin's zero-vegetable confession. 'This is a new food for me' confirms the earlier joke wasn't hyperbole. The stem-first detail is an unexpected specific touch showing Kevin has no reference point for this food whatsoever. Gabe's 'The other way' is perfectly dry.

jokes.text: Kevin mid-broccoli: 'Can I get some Cheez Whiz? Or Hollandaise?' Michael: 'No Cheez Whiz, no Hollandaise, no chocolate sauce, just eat it. Come on, here comes the airplane. There you go.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is struggling to eat plain broccoli
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of requested condiments (Cheez Whiz, Hollandaise, chocolate sauce) paired with Michael airplane-ing broccoli into Kevin's mouth like a toddler
jokes.explanation: The condiment list (Cheez Whiz to Hollandaise to chocolate sauce) escalates absurdly. Michael's 'here comes the airplane' treats a grown man like an infant. Good sustained cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Okay, I ate the fluffy part. Can I be done?' Michael: 'Let me see if you swallowed it. Open your mouth. Under your tongue.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has eaten part of the broccoli and asks to stop
jokes.punchline: Michael inspects Kevin's mouth like a parent checking a child has swallowed medicine — 'Under your tongue' — implying he doesn't trust Kevin
jokes.explanation: 'Under your tongue' is a great specific detail — the one place people hide things they haven't swallowed. The parent-child dynamic that's developed throughout this scene culminates here. Good sustained escalation.

jokes.text: After the broccoli ordeal: Kevin asks for candy; Michael refuses; then: 'I'll get him water.' / 'Oh, my God!'
jokes.setup: The broccoli scene has been traumatic for Kevin; he asks for a reward
jokes.punchline: Michael refuses candy as if denying it proves a point, while Kevin's 'Oh, my God!' at presumably the water (or continued broccoli) suggests the ordeal continues
jokes.explanation: Tail end of the broccoli sequence. Less focused than the earlier beats, more chaos than comedy. Functions as a landing pad for the scene.

jokes.text: Michael sets up an apology meeting and says 'I thought there should be an HR rep here for this' — implying Holly being HR makes his apology to Creed and Kevin somehow need oversight
jokes.setup: Michael calls a meeting to apologize to Kevin and Creed
jokes.punchline: He insists on having an HR rep present for his own apology, as if apologizing is a liability situation requiring oversight — and the HR rep is Holly, whom he's clearly also trying to spend time with
jokes.explanation: Dual-purpose joke: Michael's bureaucratic instinct to cover himself legally, and his transparent excuse to involve Holly. Both layers are character-consistent.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'It was traumatizing, Michael. I wouldn't be surprised if I never ate a vegetable again.'
jokes.setup: Michael apologizes for being too aggressive about the resolutions
jokes.punchline: Kevin frames never eating vegetables again as a trauma response — but the baseline was already zero vegetables, so it's no change whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback that lands harder because of the earlier setup. Kevin threatening 'I may never eat a vegetable again' as a trauma response is funny on its own, but devastating when you remember he already ate zero. The escalation from joke 51 through the broccoli sequence to this payoff is well-constructed. High economy.

jokes.text: Michael's apology: 'You loom so large in my heart that I crossed the line.'
jokes.setup: Michael is apologizing to Kevin and Creed for his behavior in the meeting
jokes.punchline: His apology includes the deeply strange phrase 'you loom so large in my heart' — a sincere but oddly romantic thing to say to Kevin and Creed while HR watches
jokes.explanation: Michael's unique syntax — the grandiose emotional declaration in a mundane HR meeting — is reliably funny. 'You loom so large in my heart' is a strange and specific phrase that only Michael would use while apologizing for force-feeding someone broccoli.

jokes.text: Michael to Kevin and Creed in the apology: 'you loom so large in my heart that I crossed the line'
jokes.setup: Michael is apologizing to Kevin and Creed for being too aggressive
jokes.punchline: His apology language is wildly overwrought for the recipient — 'you loom so large in my heart' to Creed, of all people, is absurdly sincere
jokes.explanation: The disconnect between Michael's language and his audience (Creed) is the joke. 'You loom so large in my heart' addressed to Creed is inherently absurd. Mild but functional.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Okay, Michael, no offense. But you need to get your own life.' Michael: 'You're right. And I hope that we can still be friends.' Creed: 'I don't think I'm there yet, boss.'
jokes.setup: Creed gives Michael unsolicited life advice as part of the apology
jokes.punchline: 'I don't think I'm there yet, boss.' — Creed playing the wounded party after being literally force-fed broccoli, delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Creed holding a grudge after being made to eat broccoli against his will and treating it as a major emotional wound is perfect Creed. 'I don't think I'm there yet, boss' has a great gravity to it. His deadpan self-righteousness is impeccable.

jokes.text: Ryan is playing guitar and a bystander asks 'Hey, it's just you. Anything you want to hear?' Ryan: 'Dave Matthews Band. No hits, deep tracks only.' Person leaves. Ryan: 'I said, no hits.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is alone with a musician or jukebox and asked for a request
jokes.punchline: 'No hits, deep tracks only' — Ryan's insufferable music snobbery; the musician apparently ignores him and Ryan restates his demand to an empty room
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ryan character joke. 'No hits, deep tracks only' is the distilled essence of insufferable hipster music snobbery. That he restates it to nobody — 'I said, no hits' — adds a perfect lonely-posturing beat. High character integration (only Ryan would say this), highly quotable, and economical. One of the episode's best character jokes.

jokes.text: Kevin interrupts Ryan's artistic monologue: 'Hey, Ryan. How's your fart project coming?' Ryan: 'That's real, real classy, Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is in the middle of saying something pretentious
jokes.punchline: Kevin derails it entirely by asking about his 'fart project' — either Kevin misunderstood something Ryan is working on, or he's trolling Ryan
jokes.explanation: 'Fart project' as a misremembering of Ryan's creative work is a great Kevin move. Ryan's offended 'real, real classy' response plays beautifully. The contrast between Ryan's artistic self-image and Kevin's interpretation is the joke.

jokes.text: Kevin claps back at Ryan's 'real, real classy': 'Hey, was it me or you that just shoved the butt end of a pound of broccoli into my mouth because Michael told me to?' Ryan: 'Me.' Kevin: 'Kevin, don't.' 'Come on.'
jokes.setup: Ryan has called Kevin classless
jokes.punchline: Kevin's comeback references Ryan literally feeding him broccoli on Michael's orders — then Ryan calmly admits 'Me' as if accepting this fully negates the accusation
jokes.explanation: Strong callback. Ryan's simple 'Me.' admitting to the broccoli incident without further defense is a great deadpan beat. The moral authority Kevin deploys here ('I'm the classless one?') is perfectly constructed.

jokes.text: Meredith announces her resolution was 'to get more attention.' Ryan immediately: 'Nope, she's lying.'
jokes.setup: Meredith reveals her resolution mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: Ryan flatly declares 'she's lying' with no explanation — implying either the resolution is made up on the spot or he knows Meredith well enough to see through her immediately
jokes.explanation: Ryan's confident, two-word dismissal is perfectly timed and economical. The joke works because Meredith's resolution 'to get more attention' is both plausible and obviously retroactive justification for behavior we've just seen.

jokes.text: Pam announces she might be pregnant mid-caffeine-discussion. Everyone reacts. Meredith: 'Oh, my resolution was to get more attention.' — reveals the resolution was actually made up on the spot in response to Pam's pregnancy news
jokes.setup: Pam mentions she might be pregnant, which draws everyone's attention
jokes.punchline: Meredith immediately claims her resolution is 'to get more attention' — revealed to be a fabricated in-the-moment response to being upstaged by Pam
jokes.explanation: Meredith immediately pivoting her 'resolution' to attention-seeking the moment Pam announces a pregnancy is perfectly in character and structurally clean. The joke reveals itself retroactively — Ryan was right that she was lying. Good misdirection and character integration.

jokes.text: Creed's cartwheel attempt — 'One, two, three. I did it! I did a cartwheel.' — followed by apparent chaos offscreen
jokes.setup: Creed has been pressured to do a cartwheel all episode
jokes.punchline: He announces he did it — and from the reaction sounds ('Oh, God!') it was clearly catastrophic rather than the 'stunning, gorgeous cartwheel' he imagined
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the cartwheel setup. Creed announces success with complete conviction immediately followed by horror reactions from bystanders. The gap between his self-assessment ('I did it!') and reality (chaos) is the classic Creed joke. The callback from earlier in the episode makes this the satisfying resolution to one of the episode's running threads.

jokes.text: Creed confessional after the cartwheel: 'Lesson learned.'
jokes.setup: Creed has just done a triumphant cartwheel
jokes.punchline: 'Lesson learned' — delivered flatly, with zero elaboration on what the lesson was
jokes.explanation: Two words. The cartwheel was the lesson — or was it? The deliberate vagueness of 'lesson learned' from Creed is perfect. It sounds like self-help wisdom but is completely empty of content. Creed's inscrutability has never been deployed with more economy. One of the episode's finest moments.

jokes.text: Andy at the roller rink met a man named Andy who 'roller skates like a Greek God' — his resolution to meet women resulted in befriending a man
jokes.setup: Andy is reporting back on his women-meeting mission at the roller rink
jokes.punchline: He met a man (also named Andy) and is genuinely enthused about it — completely missing the point of the mission
jokes.explanation: Nice subversion — Andy went to meet women and ended up making a male friend, which he describes with the same enthusiasm. 'Roller skates like a Greek God' is a great phrase. Andy's obliviousness to the mission failure is very in-character.

jokes.text: Darryl reports going to the strip club: 'I was looking at the strippers at the strip club.' Darryl then asks 'So that's it, guys?' with apparent disappointment at his own day.
jokes.setup: The men report back on their respective missions
jokes.punchline: Darryl went to the strip club he warned against, describes it in the most redundant possible way ('looking at the strippers at the strip club'), and then himself seems defeated by the outcome
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Darryl's own warning — he went anyway and apparently experienced exactly what he feared. 'I was looking at the strippers at the strip club' as the entire report is deadpan gold. His defeated 'so that's it, guys?' suggests it was not worth it.

jokes.text: 'If you want I can put on the strobe.' ALL: 'Yeah!'
jokes.setup: The men are apparently in a sad, dark space after their failed women-meeting missions
jokes.punchline: Someone offers a strobe light as the consolation activity and everyone unanimously agrees with enthusiasm — the bar for joy is now extremely low
jokes.explanation: The unanimous enthusiasm for a strobe light after a day of failures is a good group character beat — these men are easily pleased. Quick and effective.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head resolution: 'My resolution? I never want to make Holly cry again. Unless it's from laughing too hard. Or making love too beautifully.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects on his resolution after the emotional day
jokes.punchline: The sweet sentiment is undercut by two escalating exceptions — laughing too hard (acceptable), then 'making love too beautifully' — the latter delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured escalation joke. The sweet romantic note turns absurd through two exceptions, the second of which ('making love too beautifully') is both presumptuous and oddly specific. Delivered with pure Michael sincerity. Highly quotable and deeply character-integrated. One of the episode's strongest closing beats.

jokes.text: Holly alone, repeating 'we're gonna be just fine' until it stops sounding like words: 'Going to be just fine. Just fine, just fine, just fine.'
jokes.setup: Holly has told Pam she and AJ are 'just fine'; alone now, she repeats it
jokes.punchline: The repetition reveals she's trying to convince herself; 'You know how you say something over and over and the words start to sound weird?' — she's having a quiet breakdown
jokes.explanation: More emotional than comic but functions as dark-subversive cringe. The semantic satiation ('say something over and over and words start to sound weird') used to frame relationship doubt is clever. The comedy comes from the gap between her performance of confidence and this private unraveling.

jokes.text: Final scene: Creed finally doing a successful cartwheel — Michael coaches him: 'Look at where you're going to be doing the cartwheel... You know what? I'm gonna stay here as long as it takes. I really appreciate it. I'm gonna spot you.' Creed does it. 'What a rush! That's all I had to do all year.'
jokes.setup: After the failed cartwheel earlier and the apology, Michael follows through on actually helping Creed
jokes.punchline: 'What a rush! That's all I had to do all year.' — Creed's complete satisfaction with having done exactly one cartwheel as the sum total of his year's ambition, delivered with pure joy
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback. 'What a rush! That's all I had to do all year' is the ideal Creed payoff — small ambition achieved with maximal personal triumph. The warm coaching from Michael redeems the resolution-board chaos and ends on a genuinely sweet note. High character integration; this exact reaction could only come from Creed.

tmdb_overview: Michael prepares himself for the good or bad news about Holly and her boyfriend. In an effort to be an "awesome" office manager, Pam decides to put up a resolution board for everyone to post their New Year's resolutions.
